occurrences.issueTitle: 3.0CL automatic transmission slips and fails — flush is forbidden, filter is not serviceable
occurrences.howToFix: If symptoms appear, immediately switch to ONLY Acura/Honda ATF (never Dextron substitute) and start a regular drain-and-refill schedule at every engine oil change interval (6 months). Do NOT power-flush — this transmission has effectively no serviceable filter and pressurized flushing forces debris through tight passages. If slipping has already started, a transmission specialist (not a quick-lube) needs to drop the pan to check for clutch material in the fluid. Once debris is visible, only a rebuild fixes it ($2,500-3,500). Replacements/rebuilds may need a fresh torque converter — the original is a known weak point. Add an aftermarket transmission cooler at rebuild time; the factory cooling is undersized.

occurrences.issueTitle: 4-speed automatic: shift solenoid failure causes D4 light flash, missed shifts, and limp mode
occurrences.howToFix:
Drain-and-fill with Honda ATF-Z1/DW-1 (NEVER use generic Dexron — it will destroy the clutches). 
The transmission fluid in the Integra 4AT's are supposed to be changed every 3 years/36,000 mi. It can cook and wear out just like the oil in your engine.
 Pull codes with a Honda jumper or scan tool; the lock-up and shift solenoids are external, three-bolt parts accessible from the engine bay and often just need cleaning. 
A screwed up lock-up solenoid will give you a general CEL #70 (Automatic Transaxle); the solenoid is totally accessible from the engine bay and costs less than $200 to replace. It's held in place by three bolts.

occurrences.issueTitle: Engine motor mounts crack and collapse — drivetrain vibration + clunk on shifts
occurrences.howToFix: Replace mounts one at a time as they fail, not all four preemptively (the front and side mounts can last 200k+). Diagnose by having a helper rev the engine in neutral while you look — a healthy mount holds the engine still; a dead one lets the engine rock 1-2 inches. Common pattern: rear mount + passenger-side mount are the first two to need replacement, and both are visible from above without lifting. Aftermarket options range from cheap rubber ($30 each) to Energy Suspension polyurethane ($60-100, transmits more vibration but lasts forever) to Innovative Mounts billet ($100-200, used for tracked cars). For a daily-driver Integra, OEM Honda rubber or Cardone is the right balance. Total cost replacing rear + side: $80-300 in parts, 2-3 hours of labor.

occurrences.issueTitle: Ignition switch contact pitting causes engine to die when key released
occurrences.howToFix:
Replace the ignition switch electrical portion (not the cylinder/lock) — it unbolts from the back of the steering column lock housing with two screws. OEM Honda part is the most reliable choice. 
The issue is starting the car and it dies as soon as you let go of the key. After research, it became obvious it was an ignition switch issue.
 Check the under-hood main fuse and the ignition fuses before condemning the switch. Budget $50-150 for parts and 1 hour labor.

occurrences.issueTitle: Ignitor / ignition control module inside the distributor fails — intermittent or no-start
occurrences.howToFix: Test the ignitor before replacing — a multimeter check at the coil primary terminals while cranking will confirm whether the module is sending pulse to the coil. If no pulse: replace. OEM Honda module $80-150, aftermarket (Beck Arnley, Delphi) $30-80. The module sits inside the distributor cap; replacement requires removing the cap and rotor, unscrewing 2 mounting screws, and transferring the heat sink if present (Civic/Integra units may require heat sink #30121-PM5-A02 for correct fitment). Inspect the inside of the distributor cap and rotor for moisture or corrosion while you're in there — a cracked cap allows water in and causes premature module failure on the replacement. Replace cap + rotor at the same time as a preventive measure.

occurrences.issueTitle: Internal distributor failure causing stalling, no-start, and misfires
occurrences.howToFix:
Pull DTCs first — codes P1381 (cylinder position sensor) and Code 22 commonly originate inside the distributor. 
P1381 is the cylinder position sensor code, located inside the distributor.
 Replace the complete OEM distributor assembly (avoid cheap aftermarket — many fail within months). OBD1 (94-95) and OBD2 (96-99) distributors are not interchangeable. 
It is worth noting that the distributor plugs are different for each obd generation. So the obd1, and obd2 have different harness plugs.
 Budget $250-550 for a quality unit installed.

occurrences.issueTitle: Outer CV joint boot tears leading to joint failure and clicking
occurrences.howToFix:
If the boot has just torn and no elements got into the joint, regreasing and rebooting can work — a $10 boot kit vs. a $60 replacement axle is the tradeoff.
 
Reman axles run around $50 each and boot kits about $25 — AutoZone and similar carry both for the 1992 Integra 1.8L DOHC.
 
Pack outer CV joint boot with molybdenum disulfide grease, lube the spider and inside bore of rollers, ensure rollers are aligned with marks made at disassembly and install with the high side of rollers facing outward.
 Use new boot clamps (low-profile metal bands included in kit). Most owners simply swap the full reman half-shaft for under $100/side — quicker than rebooting. Always replace the axle nut and use a new transaxle retaining ring.

occurrences.issueTitle: PGM-FI main relay solder joint cracks cause hot-weather no-start
occurrences.howToFix:
Replacing the main relay is one of the easiest repairs on the Integra; it is located under the driver's-side dash, near the hood release lever and to the right of the parking brake pedal — unbolt the mounting bracket (10mm), unplug the harness, and plug in the new relay.
 
Use a quality replacement — the DA-chassis OEM part number is typically 39400-PM6-003 (verify with your VIN at an Acura dealer or parts store, as several supersessions exist). Reputable aftermarket cross-references include Standard Motor Products RY-passenger-style relays, Beck/Arnley, and Denso. Expect to pay $25-$80 for the part and avoid the cheapest generic relays — reliability matters.
 
Resoldering the cracked joints on the existing relay's circuit board has been done successfully by many owners, but requires skill with a soldering iron and may not be permanent — a new aftermarket relay is the more reliable repair.

occurrences.issueTitle: Rear lower control arm bolts seize and shear inside bushing sleeves
occurrences.howToFix:
Soak bolts with penetrating fluid (PB Blaster/Kroil) for days before attempting removal; heat the bushing sleeve with a torch. If the bolt shears, the only fix is to cut the bushing out and drill/punch the remaining sleeve from the subframe ear. 
When you are down there and replacing rusted bolts, if they are rusted on bad enough you might have to break the welded nut they go into on the front side of the subframe and trailing arms. You can get matching sized nuts and washers.
 Replace with OEM Honda bolts (M10x1.25, ~$4-9 each from the dealer). 
Diameter = 10mm, Pitch = 1.25.

This is an advanced DIY job. Some owners replace the rear as a complete pre-pressed hub assembly (commonly $80-$120 from aftermarket suppliers), which avoids press work; others source just the bearing/race and press it into the spindle/knuckle using a hydraulic shop press (or have a machine shop do it). occurrences.issueTitle: Timing belt failure on interference B18 engine bends valves
occurrences.howToFix:
Replace the complete timing belt kit: belt, tensioner, tensioner spring, water pump, cam and crank seals, and balance shaft belt where applicable.
Non-VTEC LS (B18B1) timing belt part numbers are 14400-P7J-004 or 14400-PR4-A01, paired with the 19-tooth water pump 19200-P75-003 / 19200-PT5-000 / 19200-PT5-003. The VTEC GSR (B18C1) uses timing belt 14400-P72-004 / 14400-P72-014 paired with a 22-tooth water pump.
Do NOT mix LS and GSR water pumps — the tooth counts differ (19T vs 22T) and the belts are different lengths.
Professional cost for preventive replacement: approximately $350-600. Post-failure repair (valve job / head rebuild) can reach $2,000-3,000+.

occurrences.issueTitle: Distributor shaft seal leaks oil into cap, causes misfires (P0300-P0304) on 3.5L C35A
occurrences.howToFix: There is no replaceable seal inside the distributor — the seal is between the rotating shaft and the bearing inside the cast housing. While the distributor is out, also replace the distributor cap, rotor, and ignition wires — they're cheap and you're already at the parts. Inspect the cap and rotor on the old unit for oil contamination to confirm distributor was the source. If you also see leaks elsewhere (figure-8 cooler seal, oil filter housing), address those at the same time — they share access path. Total job: 2-3 hours independent shop.

occurrences.issueTitle: AC Compressor Clutch Failure
occurrences.howToFix: Replace the AC compressor clutch assembly or the entire compressor unit. Replace the serpentine belt if scored or damaged from the seized bearing. Evacuate and recharge the AC system. Install a new receiver/drier to prevent moisture contamination.

occurrences.issueTitle: Timing belt + water pump + tensioner at 90k mi — G25A1 is interference, valves bend if it snaps
occurrences.howToFix: Full timing kit replacement: belt + hydraulic tensioner + water pump + idler + all front seals + accessory belts as one job. A complete Aisin or Allied Motor Parts kit for the G25A1 runs $150-250. Labor at an independent: $400-700. Total: $550-950. Dealer: $1,000-1,500. The job takes ~6-8 hours because the 5-cylinder is longitudinally mounted and accessory removal is fiddlier than a transverse V6. ONLY use the OEM Honda tensioner or Aisin — the import-brand tensioners on AliExpress / cheap Amazon kits routinely fail within 10k miles on this engine.
